articles.title: Serbia to vote for new president on December 27 after student movement's poll victory
articles.summary: Serbia's parliament speaker on Thursday announced that an early presidential election will be held on December 27, following the resignation of former
articles.body: Serbia's parliament speaker on Thursday announced that an early presidential election will be held on December 27, following the resignation of former president Aleksandar Vucic in September.The election comes after a student-led movement defeated Vucic's right-wing Serbian progressive party (SNS) in an early parliamentary election on October 25, reported by news agency AP.Vucic and his party had dominated Serbian politics for nearly 14 years. After serving almost two full five-year terms as president, he had stepped down to pursue the prime minister's post but was barred from seeking a third presidential term. His bid to become prime minister ultimately failed.Parliament speaker Aleksandar expressed hope that the election would offer voters a choice between strong candidates and their programmes. He also stressed the need to strengthen democratic institutions.The presidential candidates have not yet been announced. Vucic has indicated that his SNS party may not participate in the election.Although Serbia's president largely holds a ceremonial position, the office includes command over the armed forces and a role in foreign policy.However, during his tenure, Vucic was accused of concentrating power in the presidency and exercising authoritarian control. He frequently announced major government policies and chaired cabinet meetings.Following his party's electoral defeat, Vucic accused the winners of imposing what he called "revolutionary terror". His government, however, remains formally in power until a new administration is formed.The political transition has also triggered a rise in arrests of officials and police officers suspected of misusing their positions during Vucic's rule.The youth-led movement had spearheaded nearly two years of protests following the collapse of a railway station canopy in northern Serbia, which killed 16 people. The tragedy in Novi Sad sparked public anger over alleged corruption and negligence during renovation work.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Prince William shares emotional message as The Diana Award charity, founded in memory of Princess Diana, enters administration after 27 years: 'This is not the outcome any of us wanted'
articles.summary: It is a difficult moment for Prince William as The Diana Award, the charity established in memory of his late mother, Princess Diana, has been placed into
articles.body: It is a difficult moment for Prince William as The Diana Award, the charity established in memory of his late mother, Princess Diana, has been placed into administration. The organisation, which has spent 27 years recognising young people making a positive difference in their communities, announced the development, saying it could no longer meet its financial obligations. Reacting to the news, the Prince of Wales thanked everyone who had contributed to the charity's work over the years.Following the announcement, Prince William released a statement acknowledging the charity's contribution to society and the young people it had supported."The Diana Award has recognised and encouraged thousands of young people who are changing the world for the better. I want to thank everyone whose dedication and hard work helped make that possible over so many years. W," he said.In a statement published on its official website, the charity also expressed sadness over the development."Twenty-seven years ago, the Diana Awards were created to honour Diana, Princess of Wales and her belief that young people had the power to change their community, their country and the world," the organisation said.It added that more than 50,000 young people had received the prestigious Diana Award, while thousands more had benefited from its programmes and initiatives."It is with heavy hearts that we announce The Diana Award charity has been placed into administration, after independent advice made clear that the charity can no longer continue to meet its obligations. This is not the outcome any of us wanted," the statement read.The charity also thanked its supporters and the young people whose achievements had remained central to its mission. Its directors have appointed Nick Parsk of Oury Clark Chartered Accountants as joint administrator of the company.How The Diana Award kept Princess Diana's legacy aliveEstablished in 1999, The Diana Award was created to recognise young people working to improve the lives of others. The initiative emerged from a board chaired by Gordon Brown, who was then the Chancellor of the Exchequer.Beyond recognising young changemakers, the charity worked to empower young people through school-based anti-bullying initiatives and mentorship programmes. It also provided opportunities for young leaders to develop their ideas and create a positive impact in their communities.The organisation held special significance for Prince William and Prince Harry, both of whom supported its work in honour of their mother's legacy. However, neither brother nor any representative of the Royal Household held an official position within the charity.Prince William and Prince Harry's recent support for the charityEarlier this month, The Diana Award celebrated 198 young people from 44 countries at a virtual ceremony held on November 4. Both Prince William and Prince Harry sent congratulatory letters to the recipients.At the time, the charity's chief executive, Dr Tessy Ojo CBE, praised the young award winners for their courage, compassion and determination to address some of the world's most pressing challenges.The brothers have supported the organisation through various engagements over the years, taking turns to participate in its events. In 2017, they made a joint appearance at a high-profile Diana Award event at St James's Palace to mark 20 years since their mother's death.In March 2024, Prince William attended an event marking the charity's 25th anniversary, while Prince Harry joined a later engagement through a video link.The charity's annual awards have since been held virtually. Its latest announcement, however, marks a difficult chapter for an organisation that was established to carry forward Princess Diana's belief in the power of young people to bring about meaningful change.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2019, an East Riding of Yorkshire couple lifted their kitchen floor and found a cup packed with 264 gold coins; the hoard later sold at auction for £754,000
articles.summary: An astonishing discovery in Yorkshire sees a couple uncovering 264 gold coins worth £754,000 beneath their kitchen floor, revealing a historical hoard from the 17th and 18th centuries.
articles.body: Many people dream of finding buried treasures in their homes, and one British couple did when they lifted their kitchen floor. In July 2019, a couple from Ellerby, East Riding of Yorkshire, made an extraordinary discovery, uncovering what every history buff dreams of: a cup full of gold coins hidden beneath the floorboards.Containing 264 gold coins minted between 1610 and 1727, the discovery, well known as the Ellerby Area Hoard, was one of the largest hoards of 17th- and 18th-century coins ever found. On October 7, 2022, the group of 264 gold coins, entirely certified by the Numismatic Guaranty Company (NGC), realized £754,000 (about $837,000) in an auction held by Spink & Son.How the hoard was discoveredThe couple found the gold hoard in July 2019 after pulling up the kitchen floorboards in their 18th-century home. While laying new flooring, they ripped off the existing floorboards and jackhammered through the concrete beneath. Nearly six inches beneath the concrete floor, they spotted what looked like an old electrical wire. Upon closer inspection, it turned out to be the rim of a salt-glazed earthenware cup, roughly the size of a soda can, with a broken handle. Inside the smallish beaker were the 264 gold coins.After finding the coins, the couple contacted the London auction firm Spink & Son, and the experts authenticated the hoard. Historians researching the home determined that the coins are believed to have belonged to a woman named Sarah Fernley, who once owned the property in Ellerby, North Yorkshire, and passed away in 1745.The main reason behind hiding gold under floorboardsAt that time, secure banks and paper money were readily available, yet Fernley chose the floorboards over a bank vault. The Bank of England had been established in 1694, but she appears to have distrusted financial institutions in favor of hoarding gold coins.Banking instability and war risks likely fueled skepticism of paper credit. The coins were heavily worn and mostly common denominations, representing accumulated currency stockpiled from everyday circulation. Among the rarest pieces was a Great Britain 1720 George I guinea (Lot 241), featuring a reverse brockage, a minting error in which the obverse was struck with an inverted mirror image of the reverse design. It was sold for a world-record £62,400 (about $69,000), over 10 times its estimate. Another notable piece was a Great Britain 1708 Queen Anne "Elephant and Castle" guinea (Lot 165), which fetched £24,000 (about $27,000), exceeding 10 times its estimate.Another Queen Anne coin, an England 1705 guinea graded NGC AU 50 (Lot 164), realized £13,200 (about $15,000), more than double its pre-auction estimate. One notable piece was an England 1675 Charles II guinea (Lot 101) on which the king’s name was misspelled as CRAOLVS instead of CAROLVS, potentially as a statement against the king's 1672 "Great Stop of the Exchequer." This coin realized £9,600 (about $11,000), more than five times its pre-auction estimate.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: 'Wish Akhilesh spent 6 months in jail': Azam Khan quips; gets witty reply from SP chief
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party veteran Azam Khan on Thursday said he wished party chief Akhilesh Yadav had spent at least six months in prison to understand
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Samajwadi Party veteran Azam Khan on Thursday said he wished party chief Akhilesh Yadav had spent at least six months in prison to understand the emotional and physical hardships of incarceration.Akhilesh Yadav responded that he had felt Khan's pain over the years, adding a light-hearted remark about the jails built during the SP's tenure.The exchange took place at the launch of the SP's manifesto for the 2027 Uttar Pradesh Assembly elections. Khan also spoke about the distress of being separated from his son Abdullah during a prison transfer and the fear that they might never see each other again.Recalling his time behind bars, Khan said he would sometimes tell Abdullah and other inmates that he wished Yadav could experience prison life, even if only for six months."My heart wished Akhilesh ji, too, could come to jail for six months, so he could know how the days and nights pass and what one goes through," Khan said.Asked by reporters about Khan's remarks after the manifesto launch, Yadav said, "He is a member of our party and our family. I have felt his pain from time to time."Yadav also responded with a quip about the prisons constructed when the SP was in power."I told Azam Khan that SP built best jails in Etawah during its tenure. We will also work on how to further improve jails in future," he said.Azam Khan recalls 'prison trauma'Khan described his separation from Abdullah during a transfer between prisons as one of the most painful experiences of his incarceration. He said the uncertainty over his son's whereabouts left him fearing that they might never meet again.The veteran leader also spoke about having to see his young son remain in prison with him for years. Earlier at the event, Yadav had assured Khan that the party would do whatever was necessary to fulfil the promises made in its manifesto.Khan's repeated stints behind barsThe 10-time MLA from Rampur served as a cabinet minister in the Akhilesh Yadav-led government between 2012 and 2017, holding portfolios including parliamentary affairs and urban development.He was released from Dasna jail in Ghaziabad on November 18 after the Allahabad high court granted him interim bail in a money laundering case registered by the Enforcement Directorate in connection with the Maulana Mohammad Ali Jauhar University in Rampur.The ED had arrested Khan on October 31, shortly after he was released from Rampur jail in another case. He had spent nearly 11 months behind bars during that earlier stint.Yadav has met Khan during some of his periods in custody. He visited him at Sitapur jail shortly after his arrest in February 2020 and again in March 2024, ahead of the Lok Sabha elections, to discuss candidate selection in Rampur and neighbouring constituencies.During Khan's latest incarceration, Yadav met him at Rampur jail on October 22, 2026, for around 45 minutes ahead of the 2027 Assembly elections.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Zohran Mamdani's rent freeze gets judge's approval; made Google founder Sergey Brin exit New York real estate fund; 'sold for just 6 cents on...'
articles.summary: A New York City judge has upheld Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s controversial rent freeze for roughly one million rent-stabilised, handing an important political
articles.body: A New York City judge has upheld Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s controversial rent freeze for roughly one million rent-stabilised, handing an important political victory to the Democratic socialist mayor whose affordability-focused housing agenda has drawn both praise from tenants and fierce opposition from landlords. As reported by The Guardian, Manhattan Supreme Court issued an order on November 25, in which Judge Brendan Lantry dismissed the lawsuit filed by a coalition of the landlord who were looking to block the rent freeze policy of Mamdani. The measure freezes rents on one-and two-year leases for rent-stabilised apartments beginning on or after October 1. This ruling from the court comes months after the policy attracted the attention from investors in New York’s multifamily housing sector, including Google co-founder Sergey Brin, whose exit from a New York real estate find at a steep loss had previously been linked to growing concerns over the future of rent-stabilised housing investments.Judge says Zohran Mamdani’s rent freeze has a “rational basis”The legal challenge was launched after New York City’s Rent Guidelines Board approved the rent freeze in June. Landlords argued that the board had relied on a flawed process and ignored evidence showing rising operating costs, including insurance, maintenance and taxes.However, Judge Lantry said the court’s role was not to determine whether the policy was wise or whether it could negatively affect the broader real estate market. Instead, the court had to decide whether the board’s decision was arbitrary, unreasonable or lacked a rational basis.The judge ultimately concluded that the landlords had “failed to establish” that the board acted in an unreasonable or arbitrary manner. As a result, the court upheld the rent freeze as valid.Zohran Mamdani calls ruling a victory for tenantsReacting to the court order, Mayor Mamdani described the ruling as a win for the New Yorkers who are struggling with the high cost of living of the city. “This is a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in,” Mamdani said in a statement reported by The New York Times. “Because housing is not a luxury. It is a basic necessity.”For those unaware, rent freeze was one of the important promises Mamdani made in his mayoral campaign. The policy majorly focuses on addressing the housing affordability in a city where millions of people are facing the increasing living costs.Judge criticises campaign pledge but upholds policyDespite ruling in favour of the freeze, Judge Lantry was critical of Mamdani’s campaign slogan to “freeze the rent”. The judge described the promise as “reckless and irresponsible”, noting that New York City mayors do not have unilateral authority to set rents on stabilised units. That responsibility belongs to the Rent Guidelines Board. Nevertheless, he found that the board, which approved the measure, acted within its authority and that its decision should stand.Sergey Brin’s exit renewed focus on investor concernsThe court victory also revives attention on the broader impact of rent regulations on investment in New York housing. Earlier report by Bloomberg revealed that Google co-founder Sergey Brin quietly walked away from a sizeable bet on New York City apartments, selling his stake in a struggling real estate fund for just six cents on the dollar. One of the world's richest man offloaded his holding back to the fund's manager, A&E Real Estate.Amphitheatre LLC, an entity tied to Brin, sold its shares in a fund holding nearly 5,900 units across Manhattan, Brooklyn, Queens and the Bronx. Many of those apartments fall under New York's rent-stabilization program. A&E confirmed the buyout without naming Brin, saying the investor "was willing to accept six cents on the dollar on their original equity investment to divest itself from the New York City multifamily sector."Fearless legend or grounded realist? articles.title: Chuck Lorre's foundation gave $10 million to help build a new Los Angeles food charity campus; the kitchen opened in February and Project Angel Food has now served its 22 millionth meal to people with serious illnesses
articles.summary: Project Angel Food, supported by a $10 million donation from the Chuck Lorre Family Foundation, celebrates serving its 22 millionth meal while expanding its facilities to further assist individuals with serious illnesses in Los Angeles.
articles.body: Project Angel Food, a Los Angeles nonprofit that provides medically tailored meals to people living with serious illnesses, has served its 22 millionth meal, marking a major milestone as it expands its facilities with support from a $10 million donation by the Chuck Lorre Family Foundation.The organisation marked the occasion on Tuesday with Los Angeles Mayor-elect Nithya Raman and Congresswoman Laura Friedman, who visited its new kitchen, prepared Thanksgiving meals with volunteers and helped deliver the milestone meal to Nicole, a local client enrolled in its diabetes meal programme.The achievement comes as Project Angel Food continues developing its new Kitchen and Campus in Los Angeles. The facility's kitchen opened in February, while construction has now begun on a second building designed to expand the charity's services, volunteer activities and research work.The Chuck Lorre Family Foundation contributed $10 million towards the project's $55.1 million fundraising target. Project Angel Food has raised $53.1 million so far, Los Angeles Business Journal reported.How Chuck Lorre's $10 million donation will support the projectThe campus project is being developed in two phases. The first includes the new kitchen, while the second involves a Community Outreach Center intended to broaden the organisation's work.Construction on the second building began last week. Once completed, it will include a demonstration kitchen, a volunteer centre, a rooftop herb garden and a research centre.The demonstration kitchen will be available to other nonprofit organisations, caregivers and clients seeking practical guidance on nutrition and food preparation. The rooftop garden is expected to supply herbs for the kitchen while also providing a shared space for the community.The research and policy institute will focus on medically tailored meals and examine how these services can be advanced through Medi-Cal and Medicare coverage.Chuck Lorre, the television writer and producer behind shows including The Big Bang Theory and The Kominsky Method, attended the groundbreaking ceremony. Speaking about his foundation's contribution, he described the organisation's work as a cause with personal significance."I've been without food; I've been without healthy food. It's nothing I would wish on anyone. It certainly shouldn't happen in this country," Lorre said. He added that being involved with an organisation working to address food insecurity was humbling.Project Angel Food CEO Richard Ayoub said the development would help position the nonprofit as a national participant in the Food Is Medicine movement, which recognises the role of nutrition in supporting people's health.Project Angel Food reaches 22 million mealsProject Angel Food began in 1989, founded by political activist Marianne Williamson. During its early years, the organisation focused largely on providing meals to people living with HIV and AIDS. Its services have since expanded to support patients with conditions including cancer, kidney failure, congestive heart failure, severe diabetes and Alzheimer's disease.The nonprofit now provides meals to more than 7,800 seriously ill people across Los Angeles each year.At Tuesday's milestone event, Raman and Friedman joined volunteers in preparing Thanksgiving meals before helping present the 22 millionth meal to Nicole, who receives food through the organisation's diabetes meal plan.Nicole said the meals taste good and help her feel better. She also praised the delivery drivers for greeting her with a smile."Twenty-two million meals, 22 million smiles, 22 million moments where our meals offer hope and healing," Ayoub said.Raman, who is scheduled to take office as Los Angeles mayor on December 14, said the organisation's work reflects the wider role food support can play in public health."A healthy city isn't just our hospitals and clinics. It's a doctor who can send a patient home knowing a good meal is on the way. It's a volunteer at the door who knows your name. Nobody spending Thanksgiving alone," she said.Raman first volunteered with Project Angel Food in 2021, when the nonprofit increased meal production to meet demand during the COVID-19 pandemic. She has since worked in its kitchen and delivered meals to clients. Tuesday's visit was her first to the new kitchen.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: A Greek couple who fell in love with San Diego during their 1974 honeymoon later opened a restaurant that served generations of customers; nearly 50 years after it began, they have announced plans to close
articles.summary: A family-owned Greek restaurant in San Diego, California, is set to close permanently in February 2027 after nearly five decades in business, bringing an
articles.body: A family-owned Greek restaurant in San Diego, California, is set to close permanently in February 2027 after nearly five decades in business, bringing an end to a culinary legacy built around traditional Greek food and family hospitality.Georgia's Greek Cuisine, which has served generations of customers since opening in 1977, announced that it would shut its doors at the end of February next year. Owners Georgia and Dennis Stathoulis said they had decided to retire as the restaurant's lease at its longtime location expires.In a heartfelt social media announcement, the family described the decision as a bittersweet milestone and thanked customers for being part of its journey."After 50 years of serving San Diego, we're retiring!" the owners said, adding that they wanted the remaining months to be a celebration of the relationships and memories built over the years.From a small North Park restaurant to a San Diego institutionThe restaurant's story began on April 14, 1977, when the Stathoulises opened their first Georgia's Greek Cuisine outlet at 3641 Madison Avenue in San Diego's North Park neighbourhood.Georgia, who was born and raised in Pyrgos, Greece, had immigrated to the US as a teenager. She later met Dennis, also known as Dionysis, in Albuquerque, New Mexico. Dennis had previously worked as an actor and stage performer in Athens before entering the restaurant business.The couple had initially moved to San Diego after visiting the city during their honeymoon in 1974. Drawn to its coastal surroundings, which reminded Georgia of Greece, they eventually decided to establish a restaurant there.Their first attempt at running a Greek restaurant in the region was Zorba's in Oceanside in 1975. However, the business struggled because many local customers were unfamiliar with Greek cuisine.The couple subsequently moved south and opened Georgia's Greek Cuisine, building the business around traditional family recipes and freshly prepared dishes.A 1978 profile in the San Diego Reader described how the couple worked as many as 16 hours a day, six days a week, preparing food and managing the restaurant. Dennis handled much of the cooking, while Georgia prepared stuffed grape leaves, bread and pastries. They also operated a catering business.The restaurant relocated to its present address at 3550 Rosecrans Street in the Midway District in 1992, where it has remained for more than three decades.Greek dishes, family traditions and decades of loyal customersOver the years, Georgia's Greek Cuisine became known for serving traditional Greek specialities, including moussaka, spanakopita, gyros, dolmades, pastitsio, lamb chops and freshly baked baklava.Flaming saganaki cheese, Greek salads, kebabs and avgolemono soup were also among the dishes that helped establish its reputation.Georgia continued to take an active role in the restaurant's operations. In a 2022 interview with the Peninsula Beacon, she spoke about preparing food herself, marinating meats daily and using fresh herbs and ingredients.The family also expanded its catering operations, serving private parties and larger gatherings. Its enclosed patio became a popular venue for family celebrations.However, the owners said the restaurant's legacy extended beyond its menu, with generations of customers becoming part of its story."Over the decades, we've had the pleasure of serving generations of families, making lifelong friendships, and sharing a little piece of Greece with San Diego," the family said in its announcement.They recalled watching customers' children grow up and later return with families of their own.Restaurant to remain open until February 2027The Stathoulises said they wanted customers to visit the restaurant during its final months, enjoy their favourite dishes and share memories from its nearly 50-year history."Whether you've been coming for decades or haven't visited in years, we hope you'll stop by and celebrate with us!" the family said.The owners have not announced an exact final date beyond February 2027 or disclosed what will happen to the restaurant's premises after the lease expires.The closure is being attributed to the owners' retirement and the end of the lease, rather than a relocation or plans to launch another restaurant.Georgia's Greek Cuisine is located at 3550 Rosecrans Street, Suite A, in San Diego's Midway District. It is scheduled to continue serving customers through February 2027, with dine-in, takeout and catering services available.The family ended its announcement with a message of gratitude to the city and its customers: "Thank you, San Diego, for 50 wonderful years of food, friendship, and family."You use AI every day. articles.title: Hundreds of flights cancelled as storm disrupts US on Thanksgiving
articles.summary: Thanksgiving travel faced fresh disruption on Thursday as storms swept across the United States, grounding hundreds of flights and triggering flood
articles.body: Thanksgiving travel faced fresh disruption on Thursday as storms swept across the United States, grounding hundreds of flights and triggering flood warnings in several states. The bad weather affected major travel routes as millions of Americans headed out for the holiday. FlightAware reported over 350 cancellations and around 700 delays across US airports.The disruption came as 81.5 million Americans were expected to travel at least 50 miles from home over a seven-day period around Thanksgiving, according to the American Automobile Association (AAA).The National Weather Service (NWS) forecast heavy rain, strong winds and major coastal flooding along the eastern US coast. Wind gusts of 50 mph or higher were expected along the Interstate 95 corridor, while New Jersey governor Mikie Sherrill declared a state of emergency. Parts of New York were also placed under emergency measures.The storm forced organisers to postpone New York City's annual Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade to Saturday over concerns about strong winds and the safety of its large balloons. Flooding affected coastal areas from North Carolina to New Jersey, forcing road closures and rescue operations. More than 500,000 homes and businesses were without power on Thursday morning, according to outage-tracking website poweroutage.us.The West Coast also faced severe weather, with Pacific storms bringing rain, strong winds and coastal flooding. King tides prompted flood warnings from Southern California to Oregon and Washington. In California's Pacifica, a large wave tore down part of a city pier on Wednesday.Parts of Missouri and Illinois were under winter storm warnings, with up to 13 inches of snow forecast around St Louis.The flight disruptions followed an incident at Miami International Airport on Wednesday, when a FedEx aircraft overran a runway while landing. The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) briefly grounded all flights heading to the airport. No injuries were reported, and the agency is investigating.FedEx said one of its flights had “experienced an issue upon landing”.“We are grateful that our crew is safe and there are no reported injuries. We are coordinating closely with investigating authorities, and any additional questions should be referred to the FAA,” BBC quoted FedEx statement as saying.The FAA had earlier warned that delays across the country were possible “throughout the week” because of forecast rain and wind. articles.title: Burnham says UK net migration now under 'sufficient' control
articles.summary: It comes after annual net migration fell to 77,000 - the lowest level this century, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.
articles.body:
Andy Burnham said he believes there is now a "sufficient degree of control" of net migration in the UK after it fell to 77,000 in the year to the end of June.

The prime minister said the country is "getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see" but added that there was more work to do.

The Office for National Statistics (ONS) said it is the lowest recorded net migration estimate since 1997, excluding the coronavirus pandemic.

The Conservatives said the fall was "mainly a result of changes" they made in government, while Reform UK said the figures were "no cause for celebration".

UK net migration at lowest level since 1997 as asylum claims also fall

Track UK's latest migration numbers - net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

What are the planned changes to immigration rules?

Net migration is a measure of how many extra people are added to the population in a given year.

An estimated 738,000 people immigrated to the UK in the year to June while 661,000 emigrated, according to the ONS.

In the previous 12 months, UK net migration was recorded as 204,000. It peaked at 944,000 in the year to March 2023.

The 77,000 net migration figure released on Thursday comes more than 16 years after former Conservative leader David Cameron pledged to cut it to below 100,000 before he came to power in 2010.

Speaking to broadcasters, Burnham said: "These figures begin to answer what the public has been saying, we want to see much greater control over the system.

"I'm not going to say all of the work is done and I don't want to appear complacent, but I think we're finally, as a country, getting into the position that the public has long wanted to see."

It was put to Burnham that some people may argue this was a "benefit of Brexit", in light of his desire to explore closer ties with the European Union .

Asked if freedom of movement should be up for discussion as part of the UK's future relationship with the EU, Burnham said in his reply: "I don't think you can say that Brexit did anything other than weaken control of immigration in this country."

The ONS said net migration had "fallen to levels not typically seen since the 1990s".

The biggest factors in Thursday's record low were falls in the arrivals of people coming from outside Europe in three major categories of migration: The number of people coming to the UK to work fell by 45,000, asylum claims fell by 19,000 and the total number of students fell by 33,000.

A fall had been expected because of the tightening of visas rules that began under the previous Conservative government which was then continued by Labour from July 2024.

Shadow home secretary Chris Philp argued the Conservatives should receive credit for the decrease in net migration.

He added: "We now need to go even further with an annual legally binding inward migration cap, set by Parliament, at far lower levels.

"British and European people are leaving in their droves because of Labour's high taxes whilst non-EU immigration remains far too high."

Liberal Democrat asylum and immigration spokesman Paul Kohler said Britain faces "serious demographic and economic challenges, and urgently needs a proper immigration plan to support our economy and public services".

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage welcomed the drop in numbers, but said he was concerned about "a lot of high skilled big tax paying people" leaving the UK and being replaced by people "who are paying far less in tax".

Meanwhile, his party's Treasury spokesman Robert Jenrick said the fall "came about solely because I went to see Rishi Sunak" in 2023 whilst an immigration minister in the Conservative former prime minister's government.

Jenrick, who defected to Reform earlier this year, told the BBC: "I threatened to resign unless he made a series of changes. He did".

"And as a result of those changes to the immigration system, we've got where we are today".

But he added that the changes "didn't go as far as I wanted to," adding this had been behind his resignation from the Tory government a few days later.

A Green Party spokesperson said: "Creating a harsh environment for migrants and asylum seekers is not a measure of success."

articles.summary: In a big development on defence collaboration, India and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday decided to “accelerate co-development and co-production of
articles.body: In a big development on defence collaboration, India and the United Arab Emirates on Thursday decided to “accelerate co-development and co-production of next-generation defence equipment” at 14th Joint Defence Cooperation Committee (JDCC) meeting in Abu Dhabi.During defence secretary Rajesh Kumar Singh’s UAE visit, both sides have "agreed to enhance bilateral defence ties under a wide range of areas, specifically defence industry, defence innovation and advanced technology, AI, cyber, military training and maritime safety," a defence ministry's release said.The 14th JDCC meeting was co-chaired by Singh and under-secretary, ministry of defence, UAE Lt Gen Ibrahim Nasser M Al Alawi. They decided to review the progress made in defence cooperation at regular intervals. The meeting provided strategic direction to the initiatives laid out in the India-UAE Strategic Defence Partnership Framework signed in May during the visit of PM Modi to the UAE. The Indian delegation comprised representatives from the department of defence, Indian defence forces, National Security Council Secretariat and MEA.It is believed that both nations are prioritising joint development of drone technologies, including systems tailored for naval and coastal defence. They also want to have joint efforts to cover precision-guided munitions and missile systems, building on UAE interest in Indian platforms like Akash surface-to-air missile and Pinaka rocket systems. Cooperation is likely to include joint development, construction, refit, and maintenance of naval vessels to bolster maritime security. Joint manufacturing is modelled on existing industry partnerships such as collaboration between India's ICOMM and UAE's CARACAL to produce modern small arms.India is boosting defence ties with the UAE to secure vital maritime trade routes and energy supplies, protect millions of Indian expatriates, expand defence manufacturing and exports, and navigate shifting West Asian security dynamics.To facilitate business-to-business (B2B) partnerships, a team from the Indian defence industry also accompanied the JDCC delegation. A B2B interaction between defence industries of the two countries was held on the sidelines of the meeting. The Indian defence industry delegation visited Tawazun Industrial Park and held a meeting with the Tawazun Economic Council, UAE, to explore potential areas of mutual cooperation with their UAE counterparts.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Huw Edwards gives first interviews since child abuse image conviction
articles.summary: Minister Anna Turley said she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, while Channel 4 has insisted it "holds Edwards to account".
articles.body:
Disgraced former BBC News presenter Huw Edwards has given his first interviews since being convicted in 2024 for making indecent images of children.

Edwards is seen saying he believes "silence is toxic" in a clip of a podcast released by the Observer newspaper, and he has also been interviewed for a Channel 4 documentary.

A government minister, Anna Turley, told LBC she was "deeply uncomfortable" with the interviews, and that "for too long, so many of these people in the public eye have been able to have a sort of free pass".

Channel 4 has defended the documentary. A spokesperson told the BBC that a "highly experienced director" holds Edwards to account with "no questions off limits, revealing his account of what led to his offending and very public downfall".

Edwards, formerly the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.

During the court case, Edwards admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp – including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

In a trailer for the Channel 4 programme, director Patrick Forbes asks what he was doing, to which Edwards replies: "Oh, you want me to analyse what I was doing? I mean, seriously?"

Asked again, he replies: "I'd lost the plot."

The interviewer challenges him by saying: "Well, come on," to which Edwards angrily replies: "No, not come on."

Despite that apparent combative stance, Edwards wrote on his blog on Thursday: "I want viewers to know that I did not avoid a single question, and that I answered each as honestly as I could, including those about deeply personal matters: my relationships, my temperament, my sexuality."

Explaining his reasons for giving the interviews, he said: "My difficulties became front-page news, and the account that took hold was, in places, misleading or simply untrue.

"Those promoting false narratives are also, unsurprisingly, the ones questioning my right to set the record straight.

"I was left with a choice: to let that faulty account stand forever, or to offer my own."

In a statement, Forbes said it was "an important film to make".

"It's rare to find a subject that touches on so many significant contemporary issues – whether it's celebrity culture or the power of the media – as well as enduring questions about crime and punishment," he said.

Channel 4's documentary, titled Huw Edwards - Guilty, will be broadcast on Tuesday.

In the clip for his separate interview with the Observer and its Tortoise Investigates podcast, Edwards is seen saying: "Lots of the advice I've had is just be quiet, don't say anything."

Interviewer Ceri Thomas, a former editor of the BBC's Today programme and Panorama, said he was "just deeply curious about how it was that a man of such prominence had got himself into this unbelievable, terrible fix".

The interviews have been criticised by two people who previously spoke to BBC News about allegations of Edwards' inappropriate behaviour.

One, who accused him in 2023 of sending them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel Four, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

The person, who is anonymous and not connected to the criminal case, told BBC News on Thursday that Edwards was "clearly trying to do a bit of damage repair" and they were "annoyed that he's being able to air these opinions".

Another person, who said Edwards sent them suggestive and "pushy" messages when they were working at the BBC, and was also not involved in the court case, said: "I'm pretty disgusted they are giving him the air time."

Meanwhile Rosamund Urwin, chief news correspondent for the Sunday Times, who jointly led the paper's 2023 investigation into Russell Brand, reacted to Thomas's statement by saying: "An 'unbelievable terrible fix' is quite the euphemism for someone viewing child abuse images of victims as young as 7."

The podcast will be released on Tuesday. Tortoise Media, which owns the Observer, has a deal to make some podcasts available on BBC Sounds, but the BBC said the Huw Edwards series would not be among them.

Channel 4 and the Observer said Edwards had received no payment for the interviews or had any editorial input.

articles.title: Louisiana landowners leased a campsite for $650 a year and found damaged water and septic systems when it was returned; an appeals court upheld $50,000 for distress but cut a $150,000 lost rent award to $2,250
articles.summary: Landowners in St Martin Parish, Louisiana, keep a $50,000 award for emotional distress after a campsite lease ended, while a state appeals court cut their
articles.body: Landowners in St Martin Parish, Louisiana, keep a $50,000 award for emotional distress after a campsite lease ended, while a state appeals court cut their lost rent grant to $2,250 and sent cleanup costs back for review. The Louisiana Court of Appeal for the Third Circuit issued its decision on 25 November 2026 in a dispute over a site leased for $650 a year. Judges kept the $50,000 award for mental anguish and loss of use and enjoyment, slashed a $150,000 lost rent award to $2,250 for three years, and threw out a $100,000 general repair and remediation award due to missing cost details.How the campsite was leasedStephanie Martin Musser, Elisabeth Martin Perino, Thomas J. Martin III and the estate of Elizabeth Martin Mandelli sued Julius “Jimmie” J. Stagg IV and Teddy L. Breaux over the land's condition. A written lease ran for three years from 1 August 2021 to 1 August 2023 at $650 per year, limiting use to a campsite and requiring tenants to return the property in its starting shape and remove additions. Landowners said the site started out clean with a working water well and septic system, but ended up with household rubbish, construction waste, burned and buried debris, and broken water and sewage gear. Their filing stated that the wellhead, pump and related parts were cut off and removed, leaving the well and septic system unusable and blocking new rentals.Evidence of waste and damageNeighbouring leaseholder Mark Proctor testified that he saw household rubbish, construction and demolition debris, containers with unknown contents, stained soil, burned spots and apparent buried waste. He said the water well was cut near ground level and left open, while a pipe to the septic tank was cut and uncapped. Proctor told the trial court environmental officials arranged removal of some surface and underground waste before work stopped short of a full clear-out, estimating a complete cleanup could top $150,000 or $200,000 without offering a detailed plan or written quote. Musser testified that tenants only had permission for campsite use, not for leaving construction waste or removing the wellhead or septic tank, and added: “Frustration. Frustration, concern. I was very concerned what the tenant might do.”Trial court awards damagesLandowners sued on 2 June 2025 for breach of the lease, seeking damages, lost rent and emotional distress. Neither Stagg nor Breaux answered or appeared at the default judgment hearing. On 28 January 2026, the trial court entered judgment against both tenants for:$100,000 for repair and remediation$5,500 to restore the water well and $4,400 for the septic system$150,000 for lost rental income$50,000 for mental anguish and loss of use and enjoyment$12,500 in legal fees and court costsStagg appealed alone, arguing the default judgment lacked sufficient admissible evidence, relied on disputed testimony or legal fees, and skipped required notice before default.Why the appeals court reduced lost rentThe Third Circuit ruled that seven days' notice was not required because the suit rested on a written lease breach rather than covered civil wrongdoing claims. Judges also found the lease, sworn statements, repair estimates and photos supported a breach finding. Yet the court rejected the $150,000 lost rent award because Musser's affidavit put lost rent starting 1 August 2024 at $2.05 a day, or $934.80 over 456 days, with no record support for the trial judge's larger sum. Appeals judges lowered lost rent to $2,250, equal to three years at $750 a year.Remediation costs sent back for reviewJudges overturned the $100,000 general repair and remediation award because Proctor offered no detailed plan or cost estimates and the landowners' lawyer acknowledged full remediation costs could not yet be calculated. The appeals court sent that issue back for a limited hearing on soil and groundwater cleanup costs to restore pre-August 2021 conditions, while leaving the $9,900 combined well and septic award and $12,500 in legal fees and costs intact.$50,000 distress award remainsThe appeals court upheld the $50,000 award for mental anguish and loss of use and enjoyment based on Musser's affidavit and testimony regarding the burned and buried rubbish, damaged septic system and cut well equipment. In its 25 November ruling, the Third Circuit amended and affirmed in part, reversed in part and ordered the limited remediation hearing while keeping the $50,000 distress award, $9,900 well and septic award and $12,500 fees in place and reducing lost rent to $2,250.You use AI every day. articles.title: Two Chinese nationals and their sons cheated Medicare and Medicaid of $55 million by billing for unnecessary medicines and paying patients to fill prescriptions: How the Queens family did it
articles.summary: Two Chinese nationals and two other members of their family have been indicted in the US over an alleged $55 million Medicare and Medicaid fraud scheme
articles.body: Two Chinese nationals and two other members of their family have been indicted in the US over an alleged $55 million Medicare and Medicaid fraud scheme involving unnecessary prescription medicines, illegal kickbacks, money laundering and tax offences.A federal grand jury in the Eastern District of New York returned the indictment on November 20 against Zhang Huang, 35, also known as Danny Huang; Yanle Huang, 38, also known as Logan Wong; Jian Xin Huang, 62; and Xiuqin Huang, 61. All four are residents of Queens, New York. Jian Xin Huang and Xiuqin Huang are Chinese nationals with lawful permanent residency in the US.According to the US Department of Justice, the family allegedly billed Medicare and New York Medicaid for medically unnecessary prescription drugs and paid beneficiaries cash and supermarket gift cards in exchange for filling those prescriptions. The defendants had previously been charged with conspiracy to pay healthcare kickbacks on September 30.How the family allegedly carried out the $55 million fraudAccording to court documents, siblings Zhang Huang and Yanle Huang were the beneficial owners of several pharmacies in Queens between September 2020 and March 2026. These included 168 DME Inc., 169 DME Inc., QS Pharmacy Inc., ROK Pharmacy Inc. and 19 Pharmacy Corp. Yanle, a licensed pharmacist, worked at multiple pharmacies, while their parents allegedly managed the day-to-day operations of the kickback scheme.Prosecutors allege that the pharmacies submitted claims to Medicare and Medicaid for medically unnecessary medicines, including topical medications and pain patches. Pharmacy employees were allegedly instructed to pay cash and supermarket gift certificates to Medicare beneficiaries and Medicaid recipients who agreed to fill prescriptions for these drugs.The indictment further alleges that Jian Xin Huang and Xiuqin Huang obtained the supermarket gift certificates, while Xiuqin prepared envelopes containing the alleged kickback payments.Shell companies and fake ownership allegedly used to hide the moneyInvestigators also allege that the family took steps to conceal its control over the pharmacies and hide the proceeds of the scheme.Zhang Huang, who is an IRS enrolled agent, tax preparer and owner of two accounting firms in Queens, allegedly used a tax preparation client's personal information to open a company and bank account without the client's knowledge or consent. The account was allegedly used to process pharmacy transactions.Zhang and Yanle also allegedly falsified documents and arranged for straw owners to conceal their ownership and control of the pharmacies. Zhang is accused of routing millions of dollars in fraud proceeds through multiple shell companies to hide the source of the money and evade taxes.According to the indictment, the family used the alleged proceeds to purchase multiple residences, financial investments, cryptocurrency and luxury vehicles. Zhang is also accused of evading federal taxes over four tax years.Government identifies more than $19 million in assets for seizureBetween September 2020 and March 2026, Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid and Medicaid Managed Care Plans paid the pharmacies more than $55 million, according to the Justice Department.The government has seized approximately $12.4 million in assets allegedly traceable to the scheme. An additional $6.7 million in real estate has been identified in the indictment as subject to forfeiture.What charges do the four family members face?Zhang Huang faces charges including conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US and pay healthcare kickbacks, paying healthcare kickbacks, concealment money laundering, aggravated identity theft and tax evasion. If convicted, he faces a maximum possible sentence of 107 years in prison.Yanle Huang has been charged with conspiracy to commit healthcare fraud, conspiracy to defraud the US and pay healthcare kickbacks, paying healthcare kickbacks and unlawful monetary transactions. She faces a maximum possible sentence of 55 years if convicted.Jian Xin Huang faces charges of conspiracy to defraud the US and pay healthcare kickbacks, as well as paying healthcare kickbacks. He faces a maximum possible sentence of 35 years.Xiuqin Huang has been charged with conspiracy to defraud the US and pay healthcare kickbacks. She faces a maximum possible sentence of five years if convicted.The case was investigated by the US Department of Health and Human Services Office of Inspector General and the Internal Revenue Service Criminal Investigation's New York office.The Justice Department has clarified that an indictment is only an allegation. All four defendants are presumed innocent unless proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in court.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Did Scotland's departing chief medical officer actually do anything wrong?
articles.summary: Sir Gregor Smith has stepped down, citing health reasons, amid a row about failures at NHS Grampian.
articles.body:
Sir Gregor Smith, who has resigned as Scotland's chief medical officer, was appointed to the role when his predecessor quit for breaking Covid rules.

He leaves the position having become caught up in a very different controversy.

Smith said he had taken a "personal decision" to stand down because he did not have the "good mental health" necessary to continue.

One government source suggested to me that Smith had taken the right decision and that it was better than anyone having to ask him to go.

John Swinney insists medical chief was not told to go amid growing NHS Grampian scandal

'My wife would still be alive if NHS Grampian had followed medical guidelines'

Chief medical officer Gregor Smith resigns on mental health grounds

He came under pressure because he knew about the 2022 report into liver and pancreas surgery at Aberdeen Royal Infirmary which identified 19 potentially avoidable deaths.

That report was never published by the Scottish government or NHS Grampian.

Politicians and journalists have not unreasonably wanted to know what he did with the information and why.

By his own account, it was almost accidental that he had any involvement in responding to the report.

He told a Holyrood committee that it was "unusual" for this kind of issue to be referred to him.

He said he was contacted by a senior official at NHS Grampian who also proposed an action plan that included temporarily suspending this type of surgery.

Smith seems to have considered the plan "appropriate". He called a wider meeting to discuss and ensured the then health secretary Humza Yousaf was briefed.

He was kept informed until surgery restarted on the advice of an external expert in May 2023 and according to what Smith told MSPs on Wednesday he was "not directly involved in any further work".

His disengagement became problematic because we now know this type of surgery was suspended on two further occasions. Cases are currently being referred to NHS Lothian.

Strictly speaking, it is not the chief medical officer's job to supervise the performance of any surgical department.

But had he chosen to keep an eye on things, or to ensure someone in the Scottish government did, some of the current crisis might have been averted.

The 2022 review certainly did not end concerns with how liver and pancreas surgery was being performed in Aberdeen.

These concerns have now been laid bare by one of the surgeons in that team, Dr Mohammed Habib, who went public last week.

That has prompted the Scottish government to order an independent review, led by an experienced KC, to find out who knew what and when, what they did and why.

Ministers are not convinced that somehow the report - or at least its key findings - could not have been made public by NHS Grampian.

They are not satisfied with some of the answers they have been given from the health board including the idea that patient confidentiality prevented them going public.

The review will have big questions to ask of officials at both NHS Grampian and in the Scottish government. It will also be able to question the role of ministers too.

Labour wants the Scottish Parliament to commission the review so that the Scottish government is not seen to be marking its own homework.

Both they and the Conservatives seem to want to expand the terms of the review to take account of other distressing stories emerging from NHS Grampian.

Dr Habib is worried about the outcomes in 62 liver and pancreatic cases where he believes there may have been either avoidable death or other avoidable harms.

There will be a full debate about what form the inquiry should take at Holyrood on Tuesday.

It's not clear how long the review process will take, what further investigations may be required or indeed if anyone else may leave their jobs over what's gone wrong in NHS Grampian and how problems have been handled.

articles.title: He wanted two 80ft oak trees cut down, but the council refused: Now a former Burberry manager is seeking £110,000 in compensation over damage to his £1 million home
articles.summary: A former Burberry manager is taking a London council to court after it refused to let him cut down two large oak trees in his garden, which he claims
articles.body: A former Burberry manager is taking a London council to court after it refused to let him cut down two large oak trees in his garden, which he claims caused more than £100,000 worth of damage to his £1 million home.Richard Martyn, a retired business consultant who moved to The Reddings in Mill Hill, Barnet, nearly 40 years ago, is seeking £110,000 in compensation from the London Borough of Barnet. The claim, brought on behalf of his insurers, relates to damage allegedly caused by the trees' roots to an extension at his property.According to a report by The Independent, one of the oak trees stands more than 80ft tall, while the other measures around 45ft. Martyn claims their roots contributed to subsidence, forcing him to spend more than £104,000 on repairs, including underpinning work.However, the council refused his application to fell the trees, citing their "special amenity value" to the neighbourhood. It is now disputing liability, arguing that removing the trees could itself have caused further damage to the property.How the two oak trees allegedly damaged his homeThe first signs of subsidence appeared in November 2017, when Martyn's young grandson noticed a crack in the living room. The homeowner subsequently hired experts to investigate the problem.In March 2018, a specialist identified internal and external cracks that were described as indicative of vegetation-related subsidence. An arboricultural report carried out the following month identified the two oak trees as the dominant vegetation contributing to the damage and recommended their removal.Martyn's barrister, David Thomas, told the Upper Tribunal in London that the roots had affected the foundations of the rear extension. He argued that the risk of further damage was foreseeable after the council refused permission to remove the trees.The legal team also maintained that simply pruning the oaks would not have been enough to prevent further damage. An engineer who examined the property in May 2019 reportedly linked its movement to the seasonal water demands of nearby vegetation, which caused clay shrinkage and subsidence.Why the council refused to let him cut down the treesThe two oak trees were protected by a tree preservation order. Barnet Council rejected Martyn's application to fell them because of their perceived "special amenity value" to the area.Outside court, Martyn described the decision as "pure madness".His barrister argued that the homeowner had taken precautions against possible root damage by paying extra for deeper foundations. The extension foundations were excavated to a depth of 1.3 metres, which was deeper than the minimum generally recommended for shrinkable soils.The legal team also argued that the trees were not particularly close to the house, with the smaller oak standing around 45ft away. Martyn had therefore not been expected to anticipate the extent of the root damage, it was argued.Council says removing the trees could have caused further damageBarnet Council is contesting the claim, arguing that allowing the trees to be removed would not necessarily have prevented the need for extensive repairs.Its barrister, James Neill, told the tribunal that felling and removing the oaks could have triggered a process known as 'heave'. This occurs when soil that has previously shrunk due to trees drawing out moisture begins to swell after the trees are removed.The council argued that this ground movement could have damaged the property and that underpinning might have been necessary even if permission to fell the trees had been granted.Martyn's legal team disputed this position, maintaining that the oaks were responsible for the subsidence and that their removal would have allowed the property to stabilise.The case is being heard by the Upper Tribunal in London. Judge Mark Higgin has reserved his decision and will deliver it at a later date.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: India-Germany submarine partnership can act as a catalyst for Indo-Pacific security: German envoy
articles.summary: With the India-Germany Project-75 India (P-75I) conventional submarine deal in CCS for final approval, Germany has reiterated its commitment to delivering
articles.body: With the India-Germany Project-75 India (P-75I) conventional submarine deal in CCS for final approval, Germany has reiterated its commitment to delivering comprehensive technology transfer under the long-term industrial partnership with India. German ambassador to India Jasper Wieck told TOI in an interview mutual trust regarding protection of sensitive technologies will be key to this partnership.Pegged at $ 8-9 billion, the proposed P-75I deal involving Germany’s TKMS and India’s Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Limited (MDL) to build 6 submarines equipped with the vital Air-Independent Propulsion (AIP) technology—which allows vessels to remain submerged for weeks without surfacing—will be one of the largest-ever defence contracts signed by India.Wieck said the project will see extensive transfer of technology in the underwater domain, not just limited to the submarines, as he highlighted overarching policy frameworks established by Berlin to guarantee reliability."Germany has committed to becoming a reliable defence-industrial partner of India. The bilateral defense industrial cooperation roadmap, which was signed in April this year, explicitly includes defense technology transfer," said Wieck.Asked about compartmentalisation and protection of sensitive submarine technology transferred to India, Wieck said technologies related to P-75I will only be shared with related Indian companies and government bodies. "Now, ultimately sharing technology with partners is always a question of trust and reliability, but here I can confirm India and Germany are definitely trusted partners in both directions," Wieck said.Speaking alongside Wieck about the technical execution of the project, TKMS global CEO Oliver Burkhard said P-75I is built around the transfer of the design of the submarine which will belong to the Indian Navy."You can't run a submarine if you haven't understood it. A few core technologies are protected in every partnership but India will get full access to that what they need to run, maintain, sustain those boats over the next 40 years," said Burkhard.Addressing India's concerns regarding TKMS' historical submarine contracts with Turkey, Burkhard clarified that each international program is strictly isolated and governed by German sovereign oversight."India does not have to worry because every program is ring-fenced. The technology, data, and intellectual property stay in that country and is protected by agreements between the two governments. The design India will receive is a highly advanced, unique-to-India boat and that has nothing to do with Turkey anymore," Burkhard said.Ambassador Wieck highlighted how the submarine agreement fits into Germany’s broader Indo-Pacific strategy, considering particularly regional security challenges and efforts to maintain rules-based maritime order."India plays a central role in the Indo-Pacific and India and Germany have a shared interest in upholding and defending the rules-based international order. And in the Indo-Pacific, that means the freedom of navigation and the security of lifelines of communication across the oceans. P75I is a long-term engagement with the potential of becoming a catalyst for deepening security and safety in the Indian Ocean," noted Wieck.Asked if India's ties with Russia might limit Germany's willingness to transfer sensitive naval technology, Wieck stressed mutual respect for sovereign choices."Each and every country around the world has its own network of partners and friends across the globe...instead of dwelling on India's partnerships with other countries, I'd rather focus on broadening and deepening the Indo-German partnership. Mutual trust, also regarding the protection of sensitive defense technology, is of course the key to that partnership," said Wieck.According to Burkhard, the submarine partnership might offer an opportunity for turning India a hub for Southeast Asian nations or others who want to join the submarine programme. "Submarines of the future can be built for other nations with, for example, a German design on one side, and on the other Indian competencies when it comes to assembly and manufacturing. A number of countries are approaching us. We are the global leaders in conventional submarines...so, if you can offer, for example, a country which is interested and it goes along with the political interests of India and Germany also to be part of a submarine building programme...it can be steered from a new hub in Asia, which will then be India for us," he said.On the need to adhere to strict delivery schedules, Burkhard emphasised TKMS’ delivery track record - citing four submarines and one frigate delivered this year - and noted that execution is a shared responsibility with MDL, with indigenous content reaching 70% on the final boat. While acknowledging past delays, he stressed confidence in meeting timelines, stating, "we are also in a delivery mode which shows hopefully some confidence that, of course, we will meet the timelines".Addressing concerns over integrating the AIP system into a new design for India’s P75I submarines, Burkhard called AIP a proven technology operated by the German Navy for over 20 years and across more than 50 submarines in service or under contract. He noted that India will own the design for P75I, making future modifications easier without having to depend on the foreign original equipment manufacturer.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: 17-year-old on Australia's Gold Coast feared her nan's stories would be lost, so she built a website where people record messages for loved ones to receive on birthdays and Christmases after they die
articles.summary: For 17-year-old Alice Footer, losing a family member also means losing access to their stories, experiences and memories.
articles.body: For 17-year-old Alice Footer, losing a family member also means losing access to their stories, experiences and memories. She began thinking about this after realising that her younger sister might never know her grandmother as well as she did.The concern eventually led the Gold Coast teenager in Australia to create FromBeyond.co, a website that allows people to record personal messages and decide when they should reach their loved ones, That's Life reported. These recordings can be scheduled for birthdays, Christmas and other important occasions, including dates that fall after the sender's death.The idea took shape during a family visit to the UK in July 2025. Alice's grandmother Merrin, then 76, lived in Surrey and the family usually got to see her only once a year. Although she had moved into a care home, she continued to share stories about her younger days and experiences with her grandchildren.During that visit, Merrin spoke about a video shown at a friend's funeral. She told Alice that she would prefer her family to remember her with laughter rather than sadness when she was no longer around. The conversation made Alice think about how her grandmother's experiences could be preserved for younger family members.After returning to Australia, Alice spoke to her parents about the possibility of recording such stories and messages. She was particularly concerned that her five-year-old sister, Violet, might not get to know their grandmother in the same way.Teenager turns the idea into a websiteAlice was in Year 10 and enjoyed studying business. She decided to explore whether a service already existed that could help families preserve personal memories in this way.Her research led her to digital legacy platforms, but she did not find one that offered the specific feature she wanted: allowing people to decide when a recorded message should be delivered in the future.She began developing a service around that idea. Instead of simply storing recordings for family members to access, the website would allow users to select dates for their messages to arrive. This could include birthdays, Christmas or other occasions that hold personal importance for the recipients.Her mother, Kellie, suggested that people could also make recordings to accompany their wills. Alice liked the possibility of giving families access to personal messages alongside other arrangements made for the future.She chose the name FromBeyond.co for the project and began working on it outside school hours. Along with her studies, she was involved in competing in and coaching jujitsu. She therefore used evenings and weekends to plan and develop the business.Her business studies teacher, Mrs Sugden, encouraged her efforts. Her parents also helped, while a friend of her father, Ben, who had experience in website development, assisted with the design.Alice wanted the service to be accessible to older users as well. She opted for a straightforward layout and larger text so that people who were less comfortable with technology could navigate it more easily.Grandparents help shape the projectAlice did not want the website to remain just an idea. She began speaking to people and recording their experiences to understand what families might want to preserve.During a visit to the UK, she approached her grandfather Stanley, 81, about making an interview recording for the platform. He agreed and spoke about taking Alice to football matches with her father when she was younger. He also spoke about his interest in football and his own family history.One point from their conversation stayed with Alice. Stanley wished he had asked his parents more questions about their lives when he still had the opportunity.She heard similar regrets from other people she interviewed. Their experiences reinforced her belief that recording family stories could help preserve details that might otherwise never be passed on to younger generations.Her grandfather Barry, 74, also became involved. He asked friends in his retirement community to try the website and suggest improvements. Their feedback helped Alice test the service with older users.Family deaths give the project a deeper purposeThe idea became more personal as Alice's family went through further losses. In June 2026, her maternal step-grandfather Mervyn died of bile duct cancer at the age of 77. Alice was grateful that she had managed to speak to him and record a video before his death.Her mother found the recording particularly moving when she watched it. The experience showed Alice how much a saved message could mean to family members after losing someone.Another loss followed in September, when Monica, her grandfather Barry's wife and her mother's stepmother, died aged 81. She had motor neurone disease, which had taken away her ability to speak.Monica could not record a video for the platform because the website was not ready at the time. For Alice, this was a reminder that people dealing with serious illnesses may not always have the opportunity to record messages later.She became more determined to make the service available to people who wanted to leave something personal for their families.Platform launches in September Alongside developing the website, Alice continued interviewing people about their lives. The conversations also gave her an insight into the choices and opportunities people sometimes wished they had approached differently.One man told her he regretted not pursuing professional cycling when he was in his twenties. He eventually started the sport in his forties.She also interviewed a couple who had spent 66 years together. They said they had no regrets about their life, particularly the memories they had made while raising children and travelling.These conversations added another dimension to Alice's project. She was not only interested in preserving messages for people who had died, but also in giving individuals an opportunity to document experiences they wanted their families to know about.FromBeyond.co went live in September. On the same day, Alice learnt that she had been nominated as a finalist in the national 2026 Women in Digital Awards.She called Merrin to share the news and told her grandmother that she had been the inspiration behind the project. Alice did not win the award but was pleased to have been shortlisted.The website currently serves users across Australia. Alice hopes to expand its reach to other countries in the future.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.
